background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: You're a frequent visitor to the [region], but this visit comes at a very turbulent time in the area, with the three Israeli teenagers kidnapped and the U.S. Secretary of State currently in [country] trying to make some order out of the mess. Do you think that the administration's foreign policy has succeeded?

background.speaker: [target]
background.text: Well, it's been a big disappointment to those of us who have followed the [region] for a long time. For me personally, I've been coming to this country for 41 years. It's the first time I've really been concerned about the relationship that our country has had with this ally. And it didn't matter. Democrat and Republican presidents alike have been, I think, very clear, forceful to the whole world that this nation was our ally, our friend, and that was an inseparable relationship. And I'm not sure the world knows that right now to the degree that they need to, and I'm not sure our ally knows that right now. So I want to make sure that we do everything possible to say that we clearly stand with them, because I believe we do. And we recognize that they are a true ally, a friend, a mirror of the kind of personal liberty, democracy, and freedom that we so cherish in our country. And it's the only country in all of this part of the world that gives its citizens that kind of freedom and empowers its women and allows people to fulfill their dreams, argue about their politics, and they are good at that. So I think it's very important that they know that we are still with them.

background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: We've heard a lot about the bad relationship between the president and the prime minister, but how much does that really affect the alliance between the two nations?

ground_truth: I think the prime minister is extraordinarily popular in our country. I think if he came here, he would win an election. That's refreshing for us to hear. We don't see that as disrespect. We see it as the kind of courageous stand that we want every world leader to take.

background.text: You've stated repeatedly in the past that you don't believe in the two-state solution. So what solution do you think the nation and the U.S. should promote instead?

So why shouldn't the world be grateful to this nation for the manner in which it allows people to think for themselves and to believe?

background.speaker: SPEAKER_00
background.text: I want to ask you a bit about the linkage between Christianity and Zionism. Just last week the Presbyterian Church voted to divest from companies that do business with the settlements. And we've been hearing a lot of reports of decline of the support of Evangelical Christians of Israel. Should Israel be worried?

ground_truth: Israel does not have a problem with most evangelicals that I know. Israel has been the target of a lot of anti-Semitic hatred, and it's irrational. The entire BDS movement is not only irrational and bigoted, but it is anti-Semitic. It's racist. And for the Presbyterian church to engage in something like this is indefensible and abominable, and it's based on lies, misunderstanding, or maybe, as one person said, dis-understanding, because it's misinformation that's intentional. And I think that's true. There are a lot of people who, for reasons that I don't understand, other than just an anti-Semitic hatred, are determined to see Israel weakened. This makes no sense to me. I want Israel to be strong. It's free. People elect their own government here. That's a good thing. That's what we wished would happen around the world. What America gets, all excited about when people vote and they have their purple fingers. And it doesn't work out real well there because the individuals aren't free. In Israel, they are. And for people to say, let's boycott and divest from Israel and let's create sanctions, that's the craziest thing I've ever seen. I'd want to invest more in Israel, put more in this country. It has a future, and its economy is growing, and it's empowering and prospering not only its people, but it's empowering and prospering even Arabs who live here.
